1061.quote_or_event: “Reliance on mortals is in vain - know this well. The Great Giver is the One Lord God.”
1061.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan tells the seeker not to lean on any human being for support, because God alone is the real Giver.
1061.tie_back: The Kural says it is ten million times better not to ask even generous friends; Guru Arjan likewise turns the needy person away from human patrons and toward the one Giver.
1061.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 281, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1061._accuracy_note: Strong fit on not depending on other people, but Guru Arjan's reason is trust in God, while the Kural's reason is self-respect.

1062.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions.”
1062.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Nanak teaches that suffering should not be blamed on anyone else, since it comes from one's own actions. This sits within the wider Sikh acceptance of hukam, the divine order.
1062.tie_back: The Kural boldly curses the world's maker if he meant some people to live by begging; Guru Nanak takes the opposite course and tells people not to blame others for their condition but to look at their own deeds.
1062.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Asa, Patti, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1062._accuracy_note: Next-best match and really a contrast: Sikh teaching accepts the divine order and would not curse the Creator, so it answers the Kural's protest rather than echoing it.

1063.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet. One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
1063.explanation: In a salok of Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak refuses respect to the holy man who lives by begging and praises the one who earns his food by work and shares part of it. This is the basis of kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing).
1063.tie_back: The Kural calls it the hardest folly to think poverty can be cured by begging instead of effort; Guru Nanak likewise rejects living by begging and points to honest labour as the true path.
1063.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1063._accuracy_note: Close fit: both reject begging and set honest effort against it, though Guru Nanak targets begging holy men in particular.

1064.quote_or_event: “Fareed begs, O Lord, do not make me sit at another's door. If this is the way you are going to keep me, then go ahead and take the life out of my body.”
1064.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi Sheikh Farid prays never to be made dependent on another person's door, and says he would rather die.
1064.tie_back: The Kural praises the nobility that will not beg even when it has nothing to live on; Farid's salok shows the same spirit, preferring death to sitting at another's door.
1064.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1380, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 42) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1064._accuracy_note: Close fit on refusing dependence even at the cost of life; Farid voices it as a prayer to God, and the Kural's image of a greatness the world cannot hold has no counterpart here.

1065.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak stayed at Saidpur (Eminabad) with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter, and ate his plain bread rather than attend the feast of the rich official Malik Bhago. He explained that Lalo's food came from honest labour, while Bhago's wealth was squeezed from the poor.
1065.explanation: The story is the best-known Sikh lesson on honestly earned food. In the popular retelling, Guru Nanak squeezed Lalo's bread and milk came out, and squeezed Bhago's and blood came out.
1065.tie_back: The Kural says even watery gruel earned by one's own effort is the sweetest food; in the Lalo story, the carpenter's coarse bread, earned by his own work, is preferred to a rich man's feast.
1065.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as summarised in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entries 'Bhago, Malik' and 'Lalo, Bhai'
1065._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on the sweetness of honestly earned food, but this is hagiography, and the milk-and-blood miracle is a later popular detail rather than history.

1066.quote_or_event: “Cursed is the life, and cursed are the clothes, of one who wanders around, begging from door to door.”
1066.explanation: In a salok of Bihagre ki Vaar, Guru Amar Das condemns the life of someone who wears the clothes of a holy man yet lives by begging from house to house.
1066.tie_back: The Kural says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even for water for a cow; Guru Amar Das likewise calls a life of begging from door to door a cursed life.
1066.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 550, Raag Bihagra, Bihagre ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1066._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the shame of begging, but the salok targets false holy men who live by alms, not someone asking on behalf of another as in the Kural.

1067.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver keeps on giving, while those who receive grow weary of receiving.”
1067.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes God as a Giver whose giving never stops, so that it is the receivers who tire first.
1067.tie_back: The Kural begs every beggar never to ask from people who hide what they have; Guru Nanak points to the one Giver who never holds anything back.
1067.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 3), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1067._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it contrasts God's endless giving with human concealment but gives no advice about whom to ask among people.

1068.quote_or_event: “The Guru is the Ladder, the Guru is the Boat, and the Guru is the Raft to take me to the Lord's Name.”
1068.explanation: In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak pictures the Guru as the safe boat and raft that carries the soul across the world's ocean.
1068.tie_back: The Kural calls begging an unprotected little boat that splits apart on the rock of refusal; Gurbani uses the same image of a boat but offers the Guru as the vessel that does not fail.
1068.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 17, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1068._accuracy_note: Next-best match built on a shared boat image; the Sikh verse is about spiritual crossing, not about begging or refusal.

1069.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
1069.explanation: In a salok in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir links greed with death and forgiveness with God's own presence.
1069.tie_back: The Kural says the heart that melts at the thought of begging is destroyed at the thought of the misers who refuse; Kabir likewise ties the grasping, refusing spirit to death.
1069.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 155) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1069._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it shares the link between greed and destruction but not the Kural's focus on the feelings of the person who has to ask.

1070.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
1070.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Asa, Guru Nanak says that hoarded wealth cannot be gathered without wrongdoing and cannot be carried past death.
1070.tie_back: The Kural bitterly asks where the life of the refuser will hide when the asker's life leaves him at the word 'no'; Guru Nanak answers that the hoarded wealth the refuser clings to will not go with him either.
1070.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1070._accuracy_note: Partial fit on the emptiness of the hoarder's position; the verse sits in Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion and is not about refusing beggars.
